title: Take a break: cloud scheduling optimized for real-time electricity pricing
review_status: full-text audit complete; one-day single-VM empirical comparison plus explicitly idealized production projection
sections_checked: historical price-peak predictor and VM pause policy
OpenStack prototype and empirical workload/meter setup
24-hour empirical energy, cost, and CPU-time results
synthetic production projections and idle-ratio sensitivity
green-instance SLA and limitations/conclusion
venue_year_verified: arXiv v1 submitted 2013-07-26; arXiv full PDF audited; DOI 10.1109/CGC.2013.25.
evidence_note: One single-threaded synthetic Fibonacci workload on one VM/server compared over 24h: ~5.3% lower measured energy and ~6.9% lower calculated electricity price, but 4 fewer CPU hours (17.6% fewer computations) due to a 4h pause. 17.1% energy/26.63% price savings are synthetic projection for idealized 200W/0W energy-proportional hardware; availability is 83.3%. Carbon impact is estimated, not directly measured.

title: An Internet of Things Framework for Smart Energy in Buildings: Designs, Prototype, and Experiments
review_status: full-text audit complete; year-long single-building observation plus short single-user prototype demonstration, no building-wide causal savings estimate
sections_checked: one-year LEED-Gold building energy traces and occupancy analysis
location-based control framework and system architecture
24-hour user-location/device prototype scenario
actual-versus-estimated energy mode comparisons
limitations and conclusion
venue_year_verified: arXiv v1 submitted 2016-03-25; journal article published in IEEE Internet of Things Journal, vol. 2(6), Dec. 2015, DOI 10.1109/JIOT.2015.2413397; full journal PDF audited.
evidence_note: Distinguishes one-year observational energy traces in one office building from a one-user 24-hour location-based prototype scenario. Prototype consumption is reported close to an estimated frugal mode; no randomized or long-term building-wide causal savings estimate is reported. The mode baseline includes estimates and results depend on building and occupant habits.

title: Resource Management for GPT-based Model Deployed on Clouds: Challenges, Solutions, and Future Directions
review_status: full-text audit complete; framework and scheduling pseudocode proposed, no executed comparative benchmark
sections_checked: resource-management characteristics and proposed QoS metrics
framework component descriptions
utilization, load-balancing, and power-aware scheduler pseudocode
resource-demand and power-estimation assumptions
future-work discussion of standardized benchmarks and metrics
venue_year_verified: arXiv v1 submitted 2023-08-05; full arXiv PDF audited.
evidence_note: Proposes a GPT-cloud framework and three placement algorithms, but reports no executed benchmark comparison, measured latency/energy/utilization outcomes, or empirical validation of estimateResourceDemand()/estimatePower(). The authors identify standardized benchmarks and more comprehensive evaluation as future needs. Treat as design proposal, not measured scheduler evidence.

title: Towards Resource-Efficient Serverless LLM Inference with SLINFER
review_status: full-text audit complete; substantial trace-driven systems evaluation with explicit SLO and hardware/workload boundaries
sections_checked: private/serverless workload motivation and CPU/GPU feasibility
SLINFER token scheduling, memory scaling, and consolidation
four-CPU-node/four-A100 experimental setup and trace construction
end-to-end results and tuned baselines
LongBench, invocation-trace, CPU/model-size sensitivity and limitations
venue_year_verified: arXiv v2 dated 2025-12-15; full arXiv HTML audited.
evidence_note: On four 32-core Intel Xeon 6462C CPU nodes plus four A100-80GB GPU nodes, the 128-model cases report 47-62% more SLO-met requests than sllm+c and 86-154% more than sllm, varying by model/comparator. Uses Azure LLM token lengths and a sampled 30-minute Azure serverless trace mapped to 32/64/128 model functions. These are capacity-under-TTFT/TPOT-SLO results, not joules/cost per equivalent answer; older non-AMX CPUs, long inputs/tight SLOs, large models, and saturated load constrain CPU-sharing gains.
